title: The Real Risk of Using Bilingual Staff as Interpreters in Healthcare
summary: Fluency alone doesn't meet Section 1557 standards. See why bilingual staff fall short and what qualified interpreter options exist. July 2026.
body_markdown:
###


It depends on whether the staff member meets the qualified interpreter standard. Under the Section 1557 final rule effective July 2024, being bilingual alone does not qualify someone as an interpreter; interpretation must be written into their job responsibilities, their proficiency must be assessed by a third party, they must complete structured interpreter training, and they must follow a professional code of ethics. Organizations relying on ad hoc bilingual staff without those four elements documented have a compliance gap, regardless of intent.


###


Research on ad hoc interpretation consistently identifies omissions, summarization, additions, and terminology errors as the most common failure modes, with ad hoc interpreters producing errors of potential clinical consequence at more than twice the rate of trained professionals. A dropped symptom, a compressed pain history, or a dosing term swapped for a rough approximation each carry the potential to change a diagnosis or a treatment decision.


###


Opalite Health is designed to work alongside certified human interpreters inside a risk-based program, not replace them. High-stakes encounters, including informed consent, end-of-life discussions, and psychiatric crises, should route to a qualified human interpreter or a documented escalation path; Opalite covers the volume of routine, unscheduled encounters where connection delays and cost make traditional services impractical. A validated Johns Hopkins Medicine study found Opalite produced more than 90% fewer major and critical errors than certified medical interpreters, though Opalite itself recommends organizations define which encounter types require human oversight before deployment.


###


Sort encounters into tiers based on clinical stakes, then assign an approved interpretation method to each tier in writing. Capture language at intake, train staff on when to escalate and how, document the language and method used in every interpreted encounter, and build a quality-monitoring process that reviews errors and near-misses. Written policies, defined escalation routes, and consistent documentation are what convert a patchwork of workarounds into a defensible compliance record.


###


The two nationally recognized credentials in the United States are the Certified Healthcare Interpreter (CHI), awarded by the Certification Commission for Healthcare Interpreters (CCHI), and the Certified Medical Interpreter (CMI), awarded by the National Board of Certification for Medical Interpreters (NBCMI). Requiring staff to hold or actively work toward one of these credentials is the clearest way to document that the Section 1557 qualified interpreter conditions are met and to give your compliance record concrete evidence to stand on.
